title: A Wife Found for Isaac
overview: Abraham sends his most trusted servant back to his family's homeland to find a wife for his son Isaac, and the servant sees the LORD's guidance in meeting Rebekah, who agrees to come.

parts.label: Abraham's solemn oath (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: Placing a hand under the thigh was an ancient way of making a very serious promise, probably tied to family and future children, though its exact meaning is uncertain. Abraham wants Isaac's wife to come from his own relatives rather than the local Canaanites, likely so Isaac would stay loyal to the LORD, and he insists Isaac himself must not leave the land God promised.

parts.label: The prayer at the well (vv. 10-27)
parts.note: The servant, never named here but traditionally thought to be Eliezer from an earlier chapter, travels to northern Mesopotamia and asks God for a sign that also reveals character, since watering ten thirsty camels was a big job. Rebekah offers exactly that, and she turns out to be the granddaughter of Abraham's brother, so the servant praises God for leading him.

parts.label: Welcomed into Laban's home (vv. 28-49)
parts.note: Rebekah's brother Laban hurries out after seeing the jewelry and hearing her story, and some readers see in his eagerness a first hint of the shrewd man he proves to be later. The servant will not eat until he has retold the whole story, a repetition that stresses how strongly he believes God arranged it.

parts.label: The family agrees, Rebekah chooses (vv. 50-61)
parts.note: The gifts of jewelry and clothing followed the custom of gifts to a bride and her family that sealed a marriage agreement. When the family wants to delay, they ask Rebekah herself, and she answers simply, "I will go," agreeing to leave her home and family for good.

parts.label: Isaac meets Rebekah (vv. 62-67)
parts.note: Covering her face with a veil was likely the custom for a bride meeting her husband, and bringing her into Sarah's tent showed she now held the place of the family's leading woman. Many Christians have read this story as a picture of a servant gathering a bride for a beloved son, pointing to Jesus and the church.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the servant's request for a specific sign is a model for how people should seek God's guidance today or simply a description of what happened in this one unique story.
think: When something works out at just the right moment, how do you decide whether it was guidance, coincidence, or something else?
